newsitem.title: UK: British election campaign gets tough and dirty.
newsitem.headline: British election campaign gets tough and dirty.

text.p: Britain's election campaign plumbed new depths of bitterness on Friday as Prime Minister John Major accused opposition leader Tony Blair of scurrilous scare-mongering over the ruling Conservatives' pension plans.
With just six days until polling day, a furious Major said it was "absolutely contemptible" for Labour to frighten old people into thinking their pension could be at risk.

Blair said Labour was perfectly entitled to put Major's manifesto under the microscope and repeated his charge that the Conservatives intended to replace the basic state pension with a privately funded scheme if they won next Thursday's election.
"Heaven alone knows how desperate their campaign must be getting if they are prepared to stoop to tactics like this," Major said at his daily news conference.

Major said he had never come across such coldly calculated scare-mongering. "This is just the politics of crude fantasy -- scurrilous, unscrupulous campaigning in order to win votes from people who they wish to frighten.
"This sort of scare is a wholly different dimension. It really brings politics down into the gutter," he said.
The six-week campaign has been hard-fought, with negative campaigning on both sides and exchanges increasingly centred on the two leaders and which one the electors can trust.
Labour's long-established opinion poll lead has barely been dented by the long election battle.
Two polls released on Friday gave it leads over the Conservatives of 16 and 18 percentage points respectively, dwarfing the 4.3 percent swing it needs to capture power for the first time since 1979.

But Labour strategists have taken a deliberate decision in the final stretch of the campaign to supplement their party's positive agenda with a raw expose of what they see as the dangers of an unprecedented fifth Conservative win in a row.
Blair, under hostile questioning at his daily news conference, denied his party was wilfully misleading pensioners.

He said the government had failed to answer key questions about the cost of its complex pension proposals, which envisage that young people starting work will build up their own personal pension fund underpinned by a state guarantee.

"We are perfectly entitled to draw attention to what a fifth term Tory government would result in," Blair said. "There is no doubt that the purpose is to replace the basic state pension with a private pension."

Labour's popularity is based on the party's move to the centre ground of British politics under Blair, leader since July 1994. In many key areas, Labour policies are almost mirror images of those of the Conservatives.
Labour's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, said the government was in near panic because of Labour's line of attack.

Major said that when he was born his father had already retired and he felt so strongly about maintaining a guaranteed state pension that he would resign as prime minister if his cabinet ever overruled him on the issue.
The row overshadowed figures showing that Britain's economic output jumped one percent in the first three months of the year.
Economists said interest rates would have to rise to cool the economy whoever won the election, but Major said Britain was set fair to enjoy steady growth as far as they eye could see.
"We've broken the boom-bust cycle," said Major, clearly exasperated that voters are not giving his party enough credit for what he called Britain's "economic miracle".
